answer: Hypothesis: In the Social-psychology domain (discipline = "Social"), both the original and replication studies primarily used student subjects — roughly 82% of original studies and ~78–81% of replication studies (lab-weighted rows: 82.0% and 78.4%; unique-study level: 83.8% and 81.1%) drew on student samples, closely matching the stated 82.4% (original) and 80.9% (replication). No other domain fits: Economics used students in 94.4% of originals and 100% of replications, and Cognitive used students in only ~71–76% of originals (while ~82–84% of its replications used students). Thus the Social discipline is the only domain in which student samples dominated on BOTH the original and replication side.

No other domain fits both sides: Economics used students in 94.4% of originals and 100% of replications, while Cognitive used students in only ~71-76% of originals (its replications at ~82-84%). Therefore, the Social discipline is the domain in which both original and replication studies primarily used student subjects.
payload.workflow: Loaded data/meta-regression_study_data_heterogeneity_in_replication_projects.csv (927 lab-level rows, 141 unique O/R pairs via 'id', 49 labs via 'lab_id'). Verified subject columns (subjects.o/subjects.r, 1 NA each), discipline, and project via value counts and crosstabs. Computed the share of 'students' for originals and replications by discipline and by project, under row-level (lab-weighted) and unique-study (deduplicated by id) weightings, plus four aggregation variants (non-NA row-level, majority vote across labs, exclusion of aggregated==True rows, first-lab-per-id). Social was the only domain close to both stated percentages under every variant; no variant or discipline-by-project subset exactly reproduced 82.4%/80.9%, so the answer rests on the unique joint match to both targets.
